title: Madison Common Council president rules out reelection, mayoral run - Channel 3000
text: MADISON, Wis. — Common Council President Sabrina Madison said Sunday that she will not seek reelection as the District 17 alder or run for mayor. Madison, who has represented District 17 since October 2022, made the announcement amid speculation that she would enter the mayoral race. Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway recently told News 3 Now in an exclusive television interview that she would not seek reelection. Madison said she has accepted a job outside Wisconsin that begins in August. "It's an opportunity that represents something different for me, and I'm excited about exploring it," she said. Alder Madison has pushed for police body cameras in the city following the fatal shooting of Corey Ruiz in July. Late last month, the common council president joined 13 other alders in voting to fire interim independent police monitor Aeiramique Glass. Madison also said she will begin studying journalism in January and looks forward to spending more time with her family. ​COPYRIGHT 2026 BY CHANNEL 3000. ALL RIGHTS RESERVED. title: 8 questions today’s election will answer in Wisconsin - The Capital Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. Today is Election Day in Wisconsin, and voters across the state and in Dane County will make decisions in key races that will determine who controls the government at the state and federal levels. The Cap Times will track election results tonight and publish preliminary results from the Dane County Clerk’s office, as well as monitor statewide results gathered by The Associated Press and other news organizations. Polls open at 7 a.m. and close at 8 p.m., though voters still in line at 8 p.m. are legally allowed to cast their ballots after the deadline. Below is a quick primer on what to watch from the results. For more information about the races on your ballot and voting today, including the location of your polling place, visit myvote.wi.gov . Voters will select either Democratic David Crowley or Republican Tom Tiffany to be the state’s next governor. This is the first time the governor’s seat has been wide open since 2010, when then-Democratic Gov. Jim Doyle retired. This time, Democratic Gov. Tony Evers, who has been governor since 2019, is retiring after two terms. Tom Tiffany appears at a "Get Out the Vote" rally at Sidelines bar in Janesville on Oct. 22. During his run for governor, Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, has been seen as a moderate in the Democratic Party. He supports policies like legalizing recreational marijuana and universal childcare but is more tepid on issues like data centers and ending the private school voucher system. Tiffany, a congressman from northern Wisconsin, is a close Trump ally and is considered one of the more conservative members of Congress, though he has tried to move to the middle more in this race, shifting his stance on issues like abortion. A big part of his platform is cutting taxes and certain regulations. Gubernatorial candidate David Crowley listens to fellow Democratic candidates’ remarks to supporters during a rally in Madison on Oct. 31. Whoever wins will have a lot of work to do in the first weeks of his tenure as governor, as the next state budget needs writing and finalizing next year. Either Crowley or Tiffany will also have to navigate a Legislature of unknown power and makeup, with a lot of turnover expected after today’s election. With a new governor will also come a new lieutenant governor. This role is largely symbolic, and its main purpose is to be second in line of succession of the governor. Democratic Secretary of State Sarah Godlewski is Crowley’s running mate, and Republican David Varnam, the former mayor of Lancaster, is Tiffany’s running mate. The new governor and lieutenant governor will be sworn in on Jan. 4. Related: How to tell Crowley, Tiffany apart on issues All 99 seats in the state Assembly and 17 of the 33 seats in the state Senate are up for grabs. Democrats are beaming with optimism that they can flip both chambers and take back control after 16 years, though the feat is smaller in the Senate. Democrats will need to gain two more seats in the Senate and six more in the Assembly — and not lose any of their existing seats to Republicans — to gain control of either chamber. One of the battleground races that will help decide which party controls the Senate is the 17th District, which dips into southern Dane County. Longtime Republican Sen. Howard Marklein of Spring Green is facing Democratic Rep. Jenna Jacobson of Oregon for that seat. Whichever party wins a majority in either chamber will have a lot of decisions to make in the coming months, as legislators set out to finalize the next state budget and work with a new governor to work on their policy priorities. Two of Wisconsin’s seats in Congress will be crucial to which party controls the U.S. House after today. In southern Wisconsin’s 1st Congressional District, Republican U.S. Rep. Bryan Steil of Janesville is running for reelection against Democratic nurse Mitchell Berman from rural Racine County. Steil has been in Congress since 2019. In western Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District, Republican U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden of Prairie du Chien is running for reelection against Democrat Rebecca Cooke, a waitress and former political consultant and small business owner from Eau Claire. Democrats see both seats as flippable this election cycle — partly with the help of newly drawn legislative maps — though their prospects are more promising in the purple 3rd District than in the southern 1st District, where a Republican has been in office for 30 years. Voters today will decide if Democratic Attorney General Josh Kaul should serve a third term, or if Republican Fond du Lac County District Attorney should take over the job. Kaul has been attorney general since 2019, and he has used his role as attorney general to serve as a stopgap between Wisconsin and Trump’s policies. He has joined dozens of multistate lawsuits against the Trump administration. Toney has been critical of those lawsuits, and if elected he said he wants to focus more broadly on public safety. The two ran against each other before in 2022, when Kaul was running for reelection for the first time. In that race, Toney lost by roughly 35,000 votes. In Dane County, 12 Assembly seats and two Senate seats are on the ballot today, and an incumbent is running for reelection in all but two of those races. Most of the seats are held by Democratic lawmakers, and almost all of them have a challenge from a candidate on the other side. Because Dane County is a Democratic stronghold in Wisconsin, it’s likely that many of these Democratic legislators will keep their seat, but today’s election will determine that for sure. One wide open Assembly seat in Dane County is in the 76th District, which Democratic Rep. Francesca Hong currently represents. Hong ran for governor but narrowly lost the Democratic primary, and she is not on the ballot to maintain her seat in the Assembly. Democrat Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford, a Madison City Council member, is likely to win the election because the district has historically been held by a Democrat, though she is running against Republican Nina Chat of Madison for the seat. The other open seat is in the 50th Assembly District, which Rep. Jacobson, the Democrat challenging Sen. Marklein, currently represents. Democratic New Glarus School Board member Bill Oemichen is facing Republican Jon Aleckson of Springdale, a retired business leader, for the seat. The midterm elections are seen as an informal litmus test on Trump, who is halfway through his last term as president. Trump has been known for being able to rally his base of Make America Great Again supporters, but less so when he isn’t on the ballot himself. Polls also show public opinion of the MAGA movement and Trump may be waning. If Democratic candidates win big today, it may signal that Trump’s power and approval are weakening even more. On the flip side, if Democrats don’t make as many gains as they hope, it could signal that Trump’s influence is still considerable. Trump endorsed Wisconsin Republican candidates Tiffany, Van Orden and Steil, but he did not step foot in the state during this election, so the results in those races will likely also show how powerful the president is when he stays away. There will also be statewide elections for secretary of state and state treasurer on ballots today. Both of these roles are largely symbolic, though the power of each seat has been a topic of discussion in recent years and on the campaign trail. Wisconsin’s secretary of state does not oversee elections like that role does in other states, and instead oversees the state’s recordkeeping and maintains official documents. Wisconsin’s treasurer oversees state public land and unclaimed property, and signs checks. The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. In the race for secretary of state, voters will choose between Republican Jay Schroeder, a real estate and stock investor from Neenah, and Democrat JoCasta Zamarripa, a Milwaukee City Council member. In the race for state treasurer, voters will choose between Republican incumbent John Leiber and Democrat Yee Leng Xiong, a member of the Marathon County Board and D.C. Everest School Board. Related: How the candidates for state treasurer, secretary of state differ There may be changes to the state Constitution after today’s election, depending on how Wisconsinites vote on three amendments on their ballots. If approved in separate ballot questions, these Republican-backed amendments would seek to limit the governor’s veto power; bar the state from closing churches during public health emergencies; and prohibit state and local government agencies from implementing so-called DEI laws.

title: Democrats win Madison in key seats - The Daily Cardinal
text: Renuka Mayadev, Mark Pocan and Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford take Madison legislative seats, holding on to Democratic-safe districts. Mayadev keeps west Madison seat Democratic Rep. Renuka Mayadev won her seat in Madison’s 77th Assembly district at 8:57 pm on Tuesday, winning against Jane McCormick with 90% of votes.  Mayadev has held the assembly seat since January 2025, when she made history as the first South Asian person to serve in the Wisconsin State Assembly. As a former Program Advisor for Maternal and Child Health at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health, she worked on improving birth outcomes in communities of color. She helped extend postpartum Medicaid coverage for women during her first term and continues to fight for healthcare reform. She is working towards stricter and more comprehensive gun laws. As the former Executive Director of the Children’s Defense Fund-Ohio, Mayadev led many movements for an end to gun violence and will continue to improve gun laws in Madison.  Mayadev has also supported legislation for climate justice, access to education for all and fair pricing of goods and services.  Final count from the district with 96% reporting are as follows: (D) Renuka Mayadev 23,471 and 89% (R) Jane McCormick 2,786  and 11% Pocan wins uncontested for Congress U.S. Rep. Mark Pocan, D-Vermont, won Wisconsin’s District 2 seat in Congress at 8:05 p.m. on Tuesday, running uncontested and receiving 60,445 votes.  Pocan is the co-founder and co-chair of the Congressional Labor Caucus , which fights to protect workers rights and connect legislators with labor unions and workers. When Madison’s State Street Starbucks workers picketed last year, Pocan met with strikers and said it's important for politicians to support labor unions.  He has criticized his colleague and Republican gubernatorial candidate U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany,R-Minocqua, for his involvement with the House Freedom Caucus, which Pocan called extremists. Pocan has also noted Tiffany’s voting record, which he said aligned with President Donald Trump 100% of the time.  Tiffany voted to pass the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a bill that Pocan voted against . The bill could cause 10.9 million people to become uninsured by 2034, according to an estimate from the Congressional Budget Office.  Since the bill passed in the House, Pocan has fought to strengthen traditional Medicare and dispel confusion surrounding private Medicare Advantage plans. He has also co-sponsored the Medicare for All bill since he was first elected in 2013.  Final count from the district with 16.8% reporting is as follows: (D) Mark Pocan  60,445 at 100%  Write-In 0 at 0%  Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford to replace Hong in east Madison seat Democratic socialist Common Council Member Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford won the seat in Madison’s 76th Assembly district at 9:27 p.m. on Tuesday, defeating her Republican opponent Nina Chat by 92%.  The seat was previously held by Rep. Francesca Hong, who lost the Democratic nomination for Wisconsin governor this summer. Martinez-Rutherford said she shares similar policies with Hong, but wants to have her own take in the legislature.  Martinez-Rutherford is an advocate for affordable housing and has supported legislation to increase housing projects in Madison during her time as alder. She has talked at length about her past experiences with homelessness and said more work needs to be done to combat it.  During her time as alder, she co-sponsored a data center moratorium bill. The moratorium prevents the zoning of new data centers until January 2027. She promised to continue regulation against data centers as an Assembly member, saying she wants to ensure “commonsense regulations on data centers.”  In 2023, Martinez-Rutherford made history as the first transgender woman to serve in Madison’s Common Council. She will now serve as Wisconsin’s first transgender Assembly member. title: These trans and nonbinary candidates just made history - The 19th News
text: By Orion Rummler , Brooke Migdon Published Share Six transgender and nonbinary candidates made history on Election Day by winning races in states that have never elected a trans person into their legislature before. These candidates will expand LGBTQ+ political power at a time when their rights are increasingly under attack nationwide. All races are called according to projections by Decision Desk HQ. Bentley Hudgins will be Georgia’s first nonbinary and first Japanese-American lawmaker after winning their bid to represent State House District 90 in east Atlanta. They easily defeated their opponent, Republican Samantha Boston, in the deep-blue district. The 19th thanks our sponsors. Become one . Hudgins, a 33-year-old democratic socialist, spent the last three years advocating for LGBTQ+ rights in the Georgia statehouse through their work with the Human Rights Campaign. But LGBTQ+ issues were not core to their campaign: They ran on affordability, expanding healthcare access and broadly protecting civil rights. Those issues are personal for them. As they had told The 19th , Hudgins faced homelessness and barriers to accessing care for cluster headaches and seizures. They were diagnosed as legally deaf at 19, and had to have their eardrums rebuilt. Many of Hudgins’ campaign goals, like raising the state minimum wage to $20 an hour or creating an earned income tax credit to give money to lower-income Georgia families, depend on whether Democrats gain enough leverage in the state House to influence policymaking. The party needs to gain 10 seats in the chamber to reach a majority — and as of Wednesday morning, that feat looks possible.  Joanna Whaley, a hospital chaplain, will be the first trans person elected to Michigan’s state legislature after winning her race for House District 2, outside Detroit. A former megachurch pastor who has spoken openly about surviving years of “conversion therapy” as a young adult, Whaley acknowledged after winning her primary in August that her victory was “a defining moment for state history,” but added that her campaign “has never been about history.” She handily defeated her opponent, Republican Ron Kokinda, with 63 percent of the vote. Whaley ran on securing fair wages for workers, supporting statewide job training programs and lowering the cost of utilities and medical debt. She was endorsed by U.S. Rep. Sarah McBride of Delaware, the only trans member of Congress, and Abdul El-Sayed, who became the nation’s first Muslim senator on Tuesday. She was also backed by progressive advocacy groups and Democrats in the state legislature. Whaley’s primary was contentious at times. In April, her Democratic opponent, former Michigan state Rep. Frank Liberati, claimed Whaley had violated state campaign law by omitting her deadname, or the name she used before transitioning, from the affidavit of identity she submitted to run for office. A county clerk denied Liberati’s challenge to Whaley’s candidacy in May. Allison Montgomery will be Alabama’s first trans lawmaker after winning her bid for state House District 25, defeating incumbent Republican Rep. Phillip Rigsby. A software engineer and lifelong Alabamian, Montgomery ran on broadening access to healthcare, strengthening workers’ rights and eliminating the state’s grocery tax. “I know the headlines tomorrow are gonna be provocative and catchy, but let’s focus on the most important part of this victory: we showed that a truly grassroots campaign that stands on its policies and its principles has a real shot in Alabama,” Montgomery said in a statement on Tuesday after her race was called. “We the people are tired of attempts to distract us with culture war issues, whether we’re in a minority group or not. We the people know corporate interests use these issues to pit us against one another while they pick our pockets.” She added: “I’m going to work especially hard for those who hate me, because they deserve a better Alabama as much as anyone.” Jaelynn Scott will be Washington’s first trans state lawmaker — and the first out Black trans state lawmaker elected in the country — after winning her bid for state House District 37 in southeast Seattle. She easily defeated her opponent, independent Evon McCorkle, a college student, with 88 percent of the vote. Scott, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, is the executive director of the Lavender Rights Project, a Black- and trans-led civil rights nonprofit based in Seattle. Her pitch to voters centered largely on affordability, universal healthcare and taxing large corporations and billionaires. In an interview with The 19th on election night, Scott said she plans to lead “with love and compassion and empathy.” “It’s pretty surreal,” she said of her barrier-breaking win. “The fact is, people that look like me and have my identity in 2026 are used to being under attack — not leading. I think it was because of what’s happening to us, and really maybe even a bit of fear about what might happen to me and my community, that inspired me to run. I never thought we would get this far.” Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford will be the first trans person elected to the Wisconsin state legislature after winning her race for state House District 76. She defeated her opponent, Republican Nina Chat, with more than 90 percent of the vote in the deep-blue district. Martinez-Rutherford, a former food service worker, comedian and small business owner, made history in 2023 as the first trans woman elected to the Madison Common Council in the state capital. She’s spoken previously about experiencing housing and financial insecurity. Martinez-Rutherford’s campaign centered largely on economic issues, promising to fight for a living wage tied to inflation, affordable housing and access to quality healthcare. “I’m honored to have made history, but that’s the last thing on my mind,” she told The 19th in an interview Wednesday morning. “It wasn’t ever about history; it was just about making sure that people are taken care of.” In a hyperlocal race that still breaks national barriers, Quinnie Perez is projected to win her seat on the Orange County Soil and Water Conservation District. This humble board lacks a budget and has little power, but Perez winning the position in Seat 1 makes her the first trans woman ever elected in Florida. Perez ran on supporting farmworkers with fair wages and safe conditions, highlighting her family history as the daughter of Mexican farmworkers, as well as wetland restoration and building green infrastructure. Several other transgender candidates still made history, although they didn’t win. They ran in deep-red, conservative districts, taking on difficult fights without any guarantee of success. Some were the first Democrats to run for their seats in decades, signaling a new energy to run for office among trans people even as their identities become increasingly politicized. Others have had their candidacies or ability to vote questioned by local authorities due to their gender identity.  After Bella Bautista decided to run for Georgia State House District 14, she went on to become the first trans woman to win a legislative primary in Georgia. Her race was a long shot: Her district hasn’t elected a Democratic state representative since 1996. She ran anyway.  She is the first Democrat to run for this seat since 2010 — and it put a target on her back. As she told The 19th , this campaign cost her privacy and peace, leaving her feeling isolated in her rural and heavily conservative district. But she said she was determined to challenge the status quo. Her campaign focused on affordability, protecting rural land and fighting data centers.  Bobby Robertson Jr., a trans woman and financial analyst, lost her race for Kansas House District 73. But she still broke barriers as the first Democrat to challenge this seat in 10 years.  She decided to run for office after the statehouse passed SB 244 , a law that invalidated thousands of trans Kansans’ drivers licenses based on gender identity, over the governor’s veto. She wrote several letters to her state representative, Republican Rick Wilborn, explaining how the law would hurt her and her family. According to Mother Jones , she asked him to meet. She never got a response. So she decided to act.  Avery Rowland, another trans woman in Kansas, ran to represent House District 2, in the bottom-right corner of the state. According to a report by Kansas Reflector , a state GOP official questioned her eligibility to vote over the state law that targeted trans residents’ drivers licenses.  Arienne Childrey previously challenged Republican incumbent Angie King in Ohio’s House District 84 in 2024 and lost. She lost again this election cycle.  Trans Ohioans have seen overt efforts to keep them off of the ballot in the state. Childrey’s ability to run for office was challenged in 2024 because she omitted her deadname on petition paperwork. She had legally changed her name years ago and had no idea about the obscure Ohio elections law that brought her candidacy into question. Aiden Swallow, a military veteran of nearly two decades, lost her bid for Arizona House District 19 to former Republican state Sen. David Gowan. Swallow previously ran for Congress in Arizona’s 6th district, but dropped out of that race last year to run for the statehouse. In this race, she faced two Republicans on the ballot as well as another Democrat, Jackie Anderson, a retired emergency room nurse. title: A Blue Tsunami and a Rainbow Wave: How the Midterm Results Will Impact LGBTQ People - Uncloseted Media
text: Spencer Macnaughton , Hope Pisoni , and Jacqui Fulton Nov 04, 2026 17 3 6 Share El-Sayed: Conlan Houston, Talarico: Antonioaesparza , Andrews: Stimpus1 , Bottoms: Executive Office of the President of the United States. Design by: Gabrielle Korein. Subscribe A blue wave? Forget about it. Last night, Democrats had such a lopsided victory with wins in Republican strongholds that months ago were thought to have been untouchable. The results have been described as a blue tsunami , an “ earthquake ” and a seismic triumph . In doing so, they flipped seven Senate seats and the House in an election that is already being touted as a rebuke of President Donald Trump. The results will have major implications for LGBTQ progress. So far, at least 20 openly LGBTQ candidates have won their races. Vermont and Virginia passed ballot measures safeguarding LGBTQ rights. The most transphobic and bigoted candidates overwhelmingly lost their races. And the balance of power in key state legislatures has shifted towards candidates who have pledged support for queer issues, meaning many of the hundreds of anti-LGBTQ bills proposed annually will have a more difficult time being passed into law. History-Making LGBTQ Representation This year's election included several historic firsts for LGBTQ representation in American politics. Chris Pappas and his husband, Vann Bentley. USA Today . Rep. Chris Pappas (D-NH) won his Senate race in New Hampshire. In an acceptance speech in Manchester, Pappas said , “I want to thank the guy next to me, my amazing husband Vann. … He’s always been by my side. Tonight, win, lose or draw, I’m the luckiest guy because I’m married to a man that I love.” Bentley Hudgins on the campaign trail. Nicole Craine for The 19th News. Hudgins won their race in Georgia’s 90th House District. They previously served as the Human Rights Campaign’s Georgia state director. Democrat Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford becomes Wisconsin’s first openly transgender legislator. Martinez-Rutherford, who won Madison’s 76th Assembly District, has called for expanding Wisconsin’s nondiscrimination law to include gender identity and expression. Jeremy Moss becomes the first openly gay man in Michigan elected to Congress. While serving as state senator, he worked on new bills that would expand LGBTQ protections. Democrat Joanna Whaley becomes Michigan’s first openly trans legislator by winning Michigan’s 2nd House District. Whaley, who ran a progressive campaign, overcame a challenge to her eligibility levied by a Democratic opponent in the primary who claimed she should have run under her deadname. Democrat Alleria Stanley becomes Maryland’s first openly trans legislator . During her campaign, she said she would pursue legal protections for LGBTQ people and families, oppose school policies that single out transgender youth and support LGBTQ-inclusive health and sex education. Jaelynn Scott. Oregon Public Broadcasting. Democrat Jaelynn Scott becomes Washington state’s first openly trans lawmaker . During her campaign, she pledged to defend gender-affirming care from federal attacks through expanded state programs and investments. Cait Conley declared victory in New York’s 17th Congressional District, though the race has not officially been called. An out lesbian, she served in the U.S. Army, led a Special Operations team and later served as the director for counterterrorism on the National Security Council. Cait Conley gives an emphatic “We did it!” as she declares victory. Eyewitness News ABC7NY . Pro-LGBTQ Campaign Promises In addition to greater representation, the election results may change policies that affect LGBTQ Americans. Candidates in tight races made campaign promises about issues including gender-affirming healthcare, transgender students and protections against discrimination. Now that the votes are in, here’s what the winners have promised to do and what the losers won’t be able to execute. Talarico gives his acceptance speech. FOX 7 Austin . James Talarico defeated MAGA Republican Ken Paxton, making him the first Democratic senator to win in the state since 1988. Talarico said he will defend LGBTQ Texans from government overreach and protect the legality of same-sex marriage. His rhetoric on transgender rights shifted throughout the campaign, leaving his exact position unclear. Talarico’s win blocked Ken Paxton, who said he would “defeat the radical transgender movement.” In addition, Paxton has opposed LGBTQ-focused content in schools. He and his supporters also released several anti-trans attack ads against Talarico, including one depicting the Senator-elect in a dress singing a musical parody about youth gender transition. El-Sayed and his wife Sarah during his victory speech. C-SPAN . Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim senator and one of the most progressive Democrats in the Senate. El-Sayed has championed LGBTQ rights: His campaign said he opposes efforts to criminalize gender-affirming care and the use of lawsuits and funding cuts to stop providers from offering it. He also pledged to fight discrimination against LGBTQ people and restore federal HIV and PrEP funding. The now-defeated Rogers, by contrast, said he would prioritize “ education not indoctrination ,” by opposing LGBTQ inclusion in education. His record in Congress includes voting against marriage-equality measures, the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act and the repeal of “Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell.” According to the Human Rights Campaign, he has also called being gay a “lifestyle choice.” Hinojosa gives her acceptance speech. CBS Texas . In a major upset, Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Greg Abbott to become the first Democratic governor elected in Texas since 1990. While Hinojosa didn’t lay out a specific LGBTQ track record on the campaign trail, in 2023 she opposed Texas’ ban on gender-affirming care for minors and proposed an amendment to make the ban expire. She is unseating Abbott’s administration, which has said that Texas agencies should reject policies it describes as “gender ideology.” As governor, he directed agencies to recognize only male and female sexes, opposed federal Title IX rules that protect LGBTQ students from discrimination and signed Texas’ ban on most gender-affirming medical care for minors. Bottoms celebrates her victory. USA TODAY . Bottoms won her election to become the nation’s first Black woman governor. Bottoms has an excellent track record on queer issues: She has said she would support efforts to strengthen statewide LGBTQ nondiscrimination protections covering employment, housing and public accommodations. Her plans also include a statewide LGBTQ advisory council, an administration official focused on LGBTQ issues, anti-bullying policies for schools, hate-crime tracking and a ban on conversion therapy for minors. During her tenure as Atlanta’s mayor, she expanded all-gender restrooms, funded trans-led organizations and helped residents access legal support for name changes and other identity documents. Jackson, meanwhile, promised to ban what his campaign calls “ideological indoctrination” in schools and has made statements opposing gender-affirming care for minors, including a campaign ad threatening jail for providers. Andrews celebrates her victory with a speech. PBS NewsHour . Andrews, whom Trump repeatedly referred to as “Tranny Annie,” defeated Trump-backed Republican Graham, becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in South Carolina since 1998. Graham, the sister of the recently deceased Lindsey Graham, has followed in his footsteps by vocally opposing LGBTQ rights—her campaign ran several anti-trans ads . Andrews has also attracted criticism on the campaign trail from LGBTQ people and advocates for releasing her own ads calling trans women “biological men” and supporting South Carolina’s ban on gender-affirming care for minors, which marked a reversal from previous statements where she decried anti-trans attacks by Republicans. Seven Senate Seats flipped for Democrats in North Carolina, South Carolina, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Maine. Governorships flipped in Ohio, Texas, Georgia, Iowa and Nevada. The House saw 29 seats flip for Democrats, including stunners in Texas, with more seats expected in the coming days. In addition to electing the next slate of political leaders, Americans also voted on a variety of LGBTQ ballot measures that addressed gender-affirming healthcare, transgender students in sports and marriage rights. Some anti-LGBTQ measures have already passed, while the results for others are still pending. Here are the results: Arizona Proposition 318 → Arizona expanded its existing ban on trans athletes to apply to essentially all sporting events, including private schools, club sports and Little League. It also banned trans people from using their gender-aligned bathrooms and locker rooms at sporting events. Colorado Proposition 134 → As of 11:00 a.m. ET, the results for a Colorado measure banning trans girls from girls’ sports in the state were too close to call. Colorado Proposition 135 → As of 11:00 a.m., the results for a Colorado measure banning gender-affirming surgeries for people under 18 and prohibiting the use of any state or federal funds, including Medicaid, for said surgeries were too close to call. Nebraska Initiative Measure 442 → Nebraska enshrined its existing ban on trans athletes into the state constitution. Vermont Proposal 4 → Vermont passed an Equal Rights Amendment to its state constitution, enshrining equal treatment under the law on account of race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and national origin as a constitutional right. Virginia Question 2 → Virginia passed a constitutional amendment removing the state’s ban on gay marriage and replacing it with new provisions enshrining marriage equality as a right and requiring all marriages to be treated equally under the law. While gay marriage was already legal in Virginia due to the Supreme Court’s 2015 decision in Obergefell v. Hodges, this amendment future-proofs marriage equality in the state in the event of that decision being overturned. Washington Initiative 001 → As of 11:00 a.m., the results for a Washington measure requiring schools to allow parents to access their children’s “ medical or health records ” and “records of any mental health counseling” were too close to call. Advocates have argued that the law could force schools to out LGBTQ students to their parents. Washington Initiative 638 → As of 11:00 a.m., the results for a Washington measure which would pass one of the most extreme trans athlete bans in the country, requiring all students looking to compete in girls’ sports to submit evidence to verify their sex, were too close to call. State legislatures have been some of the most crucial battlegrounds for LGBTQ rights—the ACLU has tracked 531 anti-LGBTQ bills in state legislatures in 2026. Several states saw swings in the balance of legislative power, which could have major implications for future lawmaking around LGBTQ issues. Democrats took control of Michigan’s House of Representatives, gaining a trifecta in the state government and possibly paving the way for pro-LGBTQ legislation to gain traction. Minnesota’s Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party also gained a trifecta in the state government. Minnesota Democrats have been some of the most proactively pro-LGBTQ in the country, passing laws to make the state a “ trans refuge ” and ban conversion therapy . This shift in power allows that work to continue without interference from Republicans. Democrats gained a trifecta in Pennsylvania’s state government, ending decades of Republican control in the Senate. This could pave the way for pro-LGBTQ legislation in the state, such as a bill introducing nondiscrimination protections for LGBTQ people that passed the House earlier this year but has been stalled in the Senate. In a major shakeup, Democrats took both chambers of the Arizona legislature for the first time in 60 years, winning a trifecta in the state government. Republicans in the state have used their legislative control to pass anti-LGBTQ legislation, including bans on trans athletes and gender-affirming surgeries for minors, so this shift in power could be consequential for LGBTQ Arizonans. Democrats also took both chambers of the Wisconsin legislature, winning a trifecta. This could pave the way for pro-LGBTQ legislation in a state that has seen relatively little activity on LGBTQ issues in recent years. Preliminary results suggest that Democrats now control both of New Hampshire’s legislative Houses. Republicans have passed multiple anti-LGBTQ bills, including bans on trans athletes and gender-affirming care for minors, so this shift could protect LGBTQ rights in the state. The state’s Republican governor, Kelly Ayotte, has a mixed track record on LGBTQ issues, having vetoed some anti-trans bills in the past despite signing others. Additional reporting by Nico DiAlesandro. title: Beyond the governor’s race: Wisconsin election results - The Badger Herald
text: Following the Tuesday election, Democrats in Wisconsin now hold a trifecta for the first time in 16 years, winning the majorities in both the State Senate and Assembly. Beyond the closely-watched gubernatorial election, resulting in David Crowley’s election , there were a number of other races on the ballot. Attorney General: The incumbent Democrat Josh Kaul defeated Republican opponent Eric Toney, the district attorney for Fond du Lac County, according to the New York Times . Kaul, who was first elected to office in 2018, has emphasized continuing the state’s environmental enforcement efforts and addressing the opioid epidemic during a third term, while Toney criticized Kaul’s lawsuits against the Trump administration . Kaul also defeated Toney four years ago by less than two percent, according to Ballotopedia . U.S. House of Representatives: All eight congressional districts were up for reelection, but the first and third districts were key races to watch. District 2, which covers Madison, is represented by U.S. Rep. Marc Pocan, D-Madison, who ran uncontested. Before the election, Republicans had a 219-214 majority with two vacancies in the U.S. House, according to Ballotpedia . In the first congressional District, Republican incumbent Bryan Steil lost to Democratic challenger Mitchell Berman, an emergency room nurse and new politician, by 52% with over 95% of the votes in, according to the New York Times . Steil has represented the district since 2019 and previously worked as a corporate lawyer, while Berman has centered his campaign on health care and lowering costs for Wisconsinites, according to Ballotpedia . In the third congressional district, Republican incumbent Derrick Van Orden, Democratic candidate Rebecca Cooke and Independent candidates Alexander Valiensi Kent and Rustin Provance ran for office, making the district the most competitive seat in Wisconsin, according to Ballotpedia. Cooke bounced back and won the 2026 election after losing to Van Orden 51% to 49% in 2024. Cooke is a small business and nonprofit owner, who campaigned on increasing the minimum wage, supporting public schools and protecting abortion rights, according to Wisconsin Watch . Van Orden is a military veteran and has emphasized his support for President Donald Trump while building his campaign on affordability and tax cuts, according to Ballotpedia . Secretary of State: Democratic state Rep. JoCasta Zamarripa won against Republican Jay Schroeder and Green Party candidate Pete Karas, according to New York Times . Schroeder has campaigned on ending the Wisconsin Elections Commission and bringing the duties under the secretary of state, whereas Zamarripa said she sees the office as a platform to protect voting rights, according to Wisconsin Watch. Zamarripa has 10 years of experience in the State Assembly and advocates for cost-of-living, workers’ rights and modernizing the record-keeping office, according to Ballotpedia. Zamarripa said that while the secretary of state position is partisan, she will be honored to serve every Wisconsinite, regardless of party affiliation, according to EagleHerald . State Treasurer: Republican incumbent John Leiber lost to Democratic candidate Yee Leng Xiong , executive director of New Beginnings for Refugees in Wausau and a member of the Marathon County Board, according to Wisconsin Watch. Xiong has served on the D.C. Everest Area school board since 2014 and has worked as the director of a nonprofit organization, according to Ballotpedia . The State Treasurer has had its powers drawn down by the legislature since 1995 , and oversees the banking of the state. Xiong has proposed expanding the treasurer’s responsibilities, while Leiber, who was first elected in 2022, built his campaign off maintaining continuity in the office. District 76 State Assembly: Democrat Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford won the District 78 State Assembly seat over Republican Nina Chat, according to Dane County election results . Martinez-Rutherford currently holds the District 15 seat on the City of Madison Common Council. District 77 State Assembly: Incumbent Rep. Renuka Mayadev, D-Madison, maintained her State Assembly seat against opponent Republican candidate Jane McCormick for District 77, according to Dane County election results . District 78 State Assembly: Incumbent Rep. Sheila Stubbs, D-Madison, maintained the District 76 State Assembly seat over Republican Henry Johnson, according to Dane County election results . Dane County Sheriff: The Dane County Sheriff election incumbent Democrat Kalvin Barrett ran uncontested. The County Sheriff is responsible for overseeing the county sheriff department. Barrett was first elected in 2022, having previously served as an officer in the Sun Prairie police department and the Dane County Sheriff’s Office, according to Ballotpedia . Dane County Clerk of the Circuit Court: The Dane County Clerk of the Circuit Court incumbent Democrat Jeff Okazaki ran uncontested.

title: Editorial | Next mayor must foster a debate on community needs - The Capital Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom. Sign up for the Opinion Roundup newsletter for weekly Madison and Wisconsin viewpoints. It’s been nearly two weeks since Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she would not be seeking a third term after a tumultuous eight-year tenure as the city’s top official. The mayor suggested that heightened threats and harassment were major factors in her decision to drop her reelection bid. And several of the candidates to replace her have condemned the rising level of threats and personal attacks. “Madison deserves a healthy public dialogue where different perspectives are welcomed, difficult conversations are encouraged, and disagreements never become personal threats," former Alder Syed Abbas said. So it is that, even as she winds down her mayoralty, Rhodes-Conway continues to frame the local discourse in important ways. Rhodes-Conway won her first two terms by wide margins. And she was broadly seen as a frontrunner in next spring’s municipal election contest. But Rhodes-Conway had her share of detractors — especially recently, as the Madison City Council made the controversial decision to fire interim police monitor Aeiramique “Meeka” Glass amid the tensions following the fatal shooting of Corey Ruiz, a 37-year-old man who was shot and killed on July 22 by Madison police. The mayor had already attracted a number of challengers at early stages of an election campaign leading up to next year’s Feb. 16 primary that will whittle the field down to the two top candidates. Those candidates will go head-to-head in the spring nonpartisan election on April 6. We appreciate the mayor’s frankness about her concerns regarding the future of the public conversations in Madison, especially her reflection that she has "always welcomed honest disagreement and invited community input." But there has been a shift in balance, she wrote in a press release, "from productive discussion to increasingly vitriolic, personal attacks from people who seem not to care about actually understanding and debating an issue. “How can any leader govern responsibly when personal attacks and baseless conspiracies carry more weight than facts?," she asked. "How can any mayor be effective when a difference of opinion is cast as unforgivable betrayal that justifies threats of violence?” Madisonians should pause and reflect on the concerns the mayor has raised. They parallel complaints from many public servants about the coarsening of our politics at the national, state and local levels. And, as the race to replace Rhodes-Conway picks up steam, everyone should look for ways to dial down the vitriol without diminishing the serious focus on issues such as housing affordability, transportation and police reform. Madisonians are passionate about refocusing on issues that concern their city, as was demonstrated by Cap Times readers who responded to our informal survey about what they want out of their next mayor. Among the issues cited by the 34 people who responded to our survey, respondents said Madison’s next mayor must focus on making the city livable, affordable and sustainable, restructuring the Office of the Independent Monitor, listening to community members from every neighborhood, reforming the police, expanding public transit, reducing the homeless population, prioritizing small businesses and working closely with Black leaders. A wide field of contenders has already stepped up, and many of them bring experience and fresh ideas to the competition. They include the aforementioned Abbas, a former member of the Madison City Council who mounted an Assembly bid several years ago; Brian Benford, also a former council member and a longtime leader and volunteer in the community; Kaleem Caire, the former president and CEO of the Urban League of Greater Madison and the founder of One City Schools; Natalia Hacerola, an artist who promises to set aside $100,000 of the mayor’s salary to help unhoused people find long-term housing; Jonny Hinds, the founder of the Monkey Bar Gym; Marcus Robert Johnson, a veteran bartender at popular spots on the east side; April Kigeya, a former Dane County Supervisor who is emphasizing transparency in government; and Larry Williams, who goes by “Ace” and has said the fatal shootings of Corey Ruiz and Tony Robinson led him to consider a mayoral run. At least one candidate we would have liked to see run, council President Sabrina Madison, announced not only will she not mount a campaign, she won’t seek reelection either. But more candidates are likely to jump into the race, including Jason Ilstrup, the president of Downtown Madison Inc. (Ilstrup’s name was mentioned more than any other as a person respondents would like to see run.) Our hope is that Madison will see a spirited — yet also thoughtful and respectful — competition to replace Rhodes-Conway. Wise candidates will differentiate themselves from the incumbent on particular issues while recognizing that many of the policies and programs she has put in place benefit the city. Some respondents, like Danielle Devereaux-Weber, 77, say they want the next mayor to continue Rhodes-Conway’s progressive agenda. Vasanth Subramanian, 34, added to this sentiment, noting he wants to see the next mayor continue the city’s commitment to sustainability, focusing on density and transit. More affordable housing construction, says Ean Carrara, 20, must be a priority. As Gail Wiseman, 67, succinctly put it: “Our next mayor must rebuild trust by spending time in our neighborhoods, listening to residents and making sure everyone has a voice in the decisions that affect them. That is how we move toward a more equitable future and a healthier, happier, and more united Madison.” There has never been any question about the mayor’s love for Madison and her desire for the city to progress. Her decision to stand down on a schedule that will allow potential successors to outline their visions for that progress is commendable — as is her desire to see her term through to its conclusion in mid-April. This is a reminder that, whether people agree or disagree with her, Satya Rhodes-Conway has taken seriously her duties not just as a mayor but as a public steward for a great American city.

title: Mayor Rhodes-Conway names man fatally shot by Madison police - WKOW
text: Madison Police Chief John Patterson was interrupted by a protester during Thursday's news conference addressing a deadly shooting involving police. MADISON (WKOW) — Madison city officials identified the man shot and killed by a police officer Wednesday as Corey Ruiz. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced Ruiz's name during a press conference Thursday. She offered condolences to his family and emphasized that no one should lose their life during an encounter with law enforcement. "I want to start first by offering my condolences to the family of Corey Ruiz," Rhodes-Conway said. "It does not matter who you are or what your past is. You should not lose your life as a result of an encounter with law enforcement," Rhodes-Conway said. Madison Police Chief said the death of Ruiz is an "open and active homicide investigation." Officers were dispatched before 1 p.m. Wednesday for a report of someone allegedly stealing bicycles and checking parked vehicles. When officers located Ruiz and tried to contact him, he fled on a bicycle through backyards. Officers confronted Ruiz again around Baldwin and Williamson streets around 1:30 p.m. Ruiz either fell off or was taken off his bicycle by officers, which is still being investigated, Madison police reported. A physical struggle ensued with officers in the middle of the street. During the struggle, Ruiz pulled out a large fixed blade knife and injured an officer, according to police. Officers deployed a Taser but it was unsuccessful, police said. The officer injured by the knife fired his gun at Ruiz at 1:35 p.m., police said. A second officer was also injured, though it's not clear how that occurred but is not thought to be by the knife. Videos posted online appear to show Ruiz going to the ground in a struggle and what sounds like three gunshots being fired by an officer from a standing position. Ruiz suffered life-threatening injuries and was taken to a local hospital. The police department was notified around 4 p.m. Wednesday that Ruiz died from his injuries. Officers at the scene attempted life-saving measures, police said. Four officers were involved in the incident, but only one officer fired his weapon. The officer who fired the weapon is a veteran officer and was treated for his injuries. Demonstrators took to the streets of Madison to protest the use of deadly force in the case. A vigil for Ruiz is being held Thursday night. All involved officers are placed on administrative leave. The Department of Justice Division of Criminal Investigation is handling the investigation.

title: History made: Madison elects Wisconsin’s first transgender lawmaker - The Capital Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford knows she is forging a new path for the state. Madison made history Tuesday night by electing Martinez-Rutherford as Wisconsin’s first transgender state lawmaker. The gravity of the moment was not lost on the new state Assembly representative as she spoke to the Cap Times at Attorney General Josh Kaul’s election night watch party. “I think about when I was a kid, had I seen people that were trans doing things like being in government and being on television and living life, I would have been able to transition a lot sooner,” Martinez-Rutherford, 56, said of waiting until her 30s to transition. “I hope that it gives kids or families of trans people hope that they can live to be adults and that their children are going to be safe because they have somebody representing them.” After launching her campaign for Assembly in October 2025, the Madison city alder told the Cap Times she considered it a privilege to break this particular glass ceiling. That sentiment holds even more true now, she said. “I can't do a lot about protecting them physically, but I can do everything I can from the state level to ensure that trans people around the state are heard, protected and able to live their lives in dignity,” she said. Martinez-Rutherford represents District 15 on the Madison City Council, first elected in 2023 and reelected in April 2025, despite having suspended her campaign that year. During that time, Martinez-Rutherford said, she learned important lessons she plans to take with her to the state Capitol. “One of the things that I'm so proud of with the city was to be able to remove credit scores for subsidized housing, so people can actually get housing,” she said. “Can't wait to do something like that at the state level that's transformative, especially for people who are struggling.” The new representative said she plans to prioritize policy she hopes will help the average Wisconsinite. “BadgerCare for all, fully funding public schools, lowering property expenses, making sure that the city of Madison gets the funding that it needs,” she said, noting she’d like to take some of the burden off of local government and school districts who have continuously gone to referendums to raise funding. Despite the fact Democrats will control both the Assembly and Senate starting in January, Martinez-Rutherford said she knows she will face personal attacks from some people in the Capitol who don’t support transgender rights and are not welcoming of her identity. The new representative said she plans to lead with kindness. “We're just people who want to have life, liberty, and be able to pursue our happiness,” she said. “I hope that people will see that and hope that people who don't agree with us or think that I'm the devil will see the person inside of me and start caring for each other a little bit more.” The 76th Assembly District was previously held by former Democratic Rep. Francesca Hong, who gave up a run for reelection in the Assembly for an unsuccessful bid for governor. It includes downtown Madison and neighborhoods on the east and north side. Martinez-Rutherford’s council District 15 represents parts of the Willy Street, Marquette and Eastmorland neighborhoods as well as some parts of Monona. Martinez-Rutherford won the race for the 76th Assembly District with 92% of the vote against largely unknown Republican candidate Nina Chat. She is one of five transgender candidates nationwide who made history Tuesday as the first elected to their respective state Legislatures — the others include Bentley Hudgins in Georgia, Joanna Whaley in Michigan, Allison Montgomery in Alabama and Jaelynn Scott in Washington.

title: Trans candidates were elected across the country as part of blue wave - LGBTQ Nation
text: The blue wave took the midterms by storm on a national level, and it also saw trans and nonbinary candidates winning state and local elections across the country, giving trans people more say over their own rights at a time when they’re politically threatened daily. While Congress is set to have the most openly LGBTQ+ people serving in its history in 2027 , elections for state legislatures and other local offices also saw big wins for LGBTQ+ candidates. “In a historic rebuke, voters didn’t just reject LGBTQ+ hate; they have elected a historic number of LGBTQ+ elected officials,” HRC President Kelley Robinson said of the election results. “The message from LGBTQ+ voters could not be any clearer: Our rights are not up for debate, our community will not be a political punching bag, and we are not going anywhere.” Here are just some of the trans and nonbinary candidates who won this week. Michigan has elected its first openly trans woman to its House of Representatives. Earlier this year, Whaley told LGBTQ Nation that before running for office, she had served as an evangelical leader and undergone conversion therapy with four different therapists over 15 years. She then transitioned in her 30s and started working at an LGBTQ+ affirming church before running for office. Whaley’s campaign made headlines when her opponent in the Democratic Primary, Frank Liberati, filed a complaint claiming that Whaley didn’t use her legal name in her campaign filings . The Michigan LGBTQ+ Caucus dismissed the attack as a “meritless, transphobic attempt to remove Joanna Whaley from the primary election ballot.” Whaley won her election with 62.5% of the vote, decisively beating her Republican challenger. Leigh Finke became Minnesota’s first out trans lawmaker back in 2022, and this week she was re-elected for a third term. Finke has made a name for herself by helping to make the state a trans refuge for gender-affirming care while being a vocal opponent of the Trump administration’s war on all marginalized communities. Earlier this year, Finke spoke to LGBTQ Nation about the ICE activity in Minneapolis and Trump’s authoritarian regime. “I don’t think that we are almost out of the muck… but I totally believe fully that this authoritarian moment will pass. This is my place, but many people in many places will have the same resolve, and the only outcome I can imagine is that this hateful effort is defeated. Now, that may take a few years or more, and when they’re gone, it’s going to take several more years to rebuild what has been broken. But 100%, I believe that we will win.” Finke beat her Republican opponent, taking 85.5% of the vote in a clear show of support for her to keep doing what she’s doing. Kansas is not currently a great place to be trans. Earlier this year, the state passed S.B.244, which barred trans people from single-sex spaces in publicly owned facilities, such as bathrooms , and prohibited updated gender markers on identification documents, invalidating those that had already been updated. That led to trans people having their driver’s licenses revoked with zero notice . Kansas Rep. Abi Boatman was a powerful voice in the House against the bill, alongside other Democrats who tried to amend it but were voted down. In the House, Boatman said , “I have sat here for five and a half hours, and listened to this entire room debate my humanity, and my ability to participate in the most basic functions of society. And from the bottom of my heart, I hope that none of you have to ever sit through something like that.” Boatman won reelection with 67% of the vote. The Republicans still hold a supermajority in both the Kansas House and Senate. In 2022, Precious Brady-Davis was the first out trans woman of color elected in Chicago history . Now, she has been re-elected alongside her colleagues, Eira Corral Sepúlveda and Beth McElroy Krikwood. Talking to LGBTQ Nation earlier this year, Brady-Davis highlighted the damage being done to the area in the name of AI, and how trans people were being scapegoated to distract voters. “I said it from the beginning of this administration, and I still stand on that today: I think the crusade against trans kids and trans people is nothing more than a distraction. We have seen the president and his family benefit off the presidency. We saw the same tech oligarchs who sat with him as he was sworn into office say that they’re going to self-police themselves when it comes to AI, which I think is a more substantial threat than the lives of trans people.” Brady-Davis and her colleagues won the election over the GOP contingent by a wide margin. Bentley Hudgins won their election in Georgia to become the state’s first non-binary representative and its first Japanese-American lawmaker. A Democratic Socialist, Hudgins has worked to advance LGBTQ+ rights with the Human Rights Campaign. Hudgins ran on a platform centered on healthcare, affordability, and broader civil rights protections, as well as raising the minimum wage and supporting lower-income Georgia families. They won decisively, receiving 92.5% of the vote against their Republican challenger. Allison Montgomery ran in Alabama’s House District 25, a district that voted for Trump in all three elections, and took on Republican incumbent, Representative Phillip Rigsby. She flipped that district with 53.2% of the vote and is now set to be Alabama’s first openly trans lawmaker. In a statement after the race was called, Montgomery said, “I know the headlines tomorrow are gonna be provocative and catchy, but let’s focus on the most important part of this victory: we showed that a truly grassroots campaign that stands on its policies and its principles has a real shot in Alabama. We the people are tired of attempts to distract us with culture war issues, whether we’re in a minority group or not. We the people know corporate interests use these issues to pit us against one another while they pick our pockets.” The executive director of the Lavender Rights Project, a non-profit supporting Black and trans civil rights in Seattle, Jaelynn Scott is now set to become the first-ever out trans member of the state’s legislature, as well as the first Black trans state lawmaker elected in the United States. In 2022, DeShanna Neal became Delaware’s first nonbinary elected official. After being re-elected in 2024, they have now been re-elected for a third term. Like Sarah McBride, the first openly trans member of the Congress, they have consistently run on a platform focused on progressive policies around housing, education, and healthcare. Not all advances happen in the biggest offices in the land. But Florida has now elected an out trans woman for the first time in the state’s history. The Orange County Soil and Water Conservation District is not a political powerhouse, but this is still a historic moment in the state. Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford has served on the Madison Common Council District 15 since 2023, but she will soon take her seat in the Wisconsin House of Representatives. The first trans person to win election to the state’s legislature, Martinez-Rutherford won her election with 92.5% of the vote. Zooey Zephyr has won reelection to the Montana House of Representatives for a third term, running unopposed. Republicans in the Montana House have previously censured Zephyr for speaking out against their anti-trans bills , leading to her working from a bench outside of the House for a time. The state continues to push anti-trans legislation , and Zephyr has her community’s report as she pushes back on those bills. title: Eight Transgender, Nonbinary Democrats Win Legislative Races - Breitbart News
text: Eight transgender or nonbinary Democrats won legislative races Tuesday, including in Alabama, Montana, and Georgia, with seven winning statehouse seats and Delaware Rep. Sarah McBride securing another term in Congress. Those elected were Allison Montgomery in Alabama, McBride in Delaware, Jaelynn Scott in Washington, Joanna Whaley in Michigan, Bentley Hudgins in Georgia, Zooey Zephyr in Montana, Leigh Finke in Minnesota, and Dina Nina Martinez-Rutherford in Wisconsin. In Alabama, Montgomery defeated Republican incumbent Phillip Rigsby in House District 25, becoming the state’s first openly transgender lawmaker. Montgomery received 53.2 percent of the vote to Rigsby’s 46.7 percent, according to preliminary results from the Alabama Secretary of State’s office. In Montana, Zephyr won reelection to House District 95 in the Missoula area without an opponent, receiving 4,761 votes, or 100 percent, according to results published by Decision Desk HQ. In Georgia, Hudgins received 27,921 votes, or 92.5 percent, defeating Republican Samantha Boston, who received 2,280 votes, or 7.5 percent, according to Spectrum News. Hudgins became the state’s first openly transgender and nonbinary legislator after winning House District 90, a heavily Democrat district near Atlanta. Scott received 87.2 percent of the vote in Washington’s House District 37, Position 2, according to preliminary returns. Whaley defeated Republican Ron Kokinda in Michigan’s House District 2 with 62.5 percent to his 37.5 percent. Both became their states’ first openly transgender women elected to the legislature. Finke received 85.3 percent to Republican Mark Born’s 14.5 percent to retain Minnesota House District 66A. In Wisconsin, Martinez-Rutherford defeated Republican Nina Chat with 92.5 percent to Chat’s 7.5 percent for an open Assembly seat. McBride, the first openly transgender member of Congress, won a second term representing Delaware with 64.3 percent, compared with Republican Joseph Arminio’s 35.7 percent. The victories came amid continuing disputes over gender identity policies, parental rights, and schools. In a post on X, Manhattan Institute senior fellow Leor Sapir argued that the transgender debate encompasses broader disagreements over institutional authority and individual freedoms. A Pew Research Center analysis published in August found that 73 percent of Americans were uncomfortable with transgender athletes competing on teams that do not match their sex at birth, including 69 percent of women. That view crossed party lines, with 91 percent of Republicans and 55 percent of Democrats expressing discomfort in the November 2025 survey. A separate Pew survey, conducted in February 2025, found that 66 percent supported requiring transgender athletes to compete according to their sex at birth, up eight percentage points from 2022. Another 49 percent supported requiring public bathroom use according to birth sex, compared with 26 percent opposed. On schools, 47 percent supported prohibiting public elementary schools from teaching about gender identity, while 34 percent opposed it. The same survey found that 56 percent supported protections against discrimination for transgender people in employment, housing, and public spaces.

title: Dane County, Madison leaders reflect on historic state election wins - The Capital Times
text: The Cap Times is an independent newsroom serving Madison and Wisconsin. Sign up for the Morning Update to receive news in your inbox each morning. Local government officials and community members in the Madison area are celebrating and reacting to David Crowley’s historic win as Wisconsin’s first Black governor and thinking about the road ahead with a Democratic majority in the state Legislature. The Milwaukee County executive ran a campaign on making Wisconsin work for every family and tackling housing, childcare and access to healthcare, and local voters who supported him said they are feeling optimistic about progress. Community members are also reacting to the three Republican-backed constitutional amendment questions on the ballot, two of which passed. Many who spoke with the Cap Times about this election said the questions were confusing and they wanted more voter education about the potential effects of the amendments passing, especially regarding the governor’s veto power. Louis Nzegwu, a Madison voter, human resources professional and youth leader, said he found the questions confusing, but he’s otherwise happy with the state election results overall. He's already looking ahead to the spring primary election. Leading up to the Nov. 3 election, Nzegwu found himself more engaged with young people of color, discussing the implications of the amendments with first-time voters who asked for his advice. He said he felt the younger crowd might not always be thinking about voting in a midterm election, and they can be more vulnerable due to the abundance of information available, especially on social media. Voter turnout in Dane County was 79%, and according to New York Times estimates, Wisconsin voters aged 18-29 made up 9% and mostly voted Democrat. Voters aged 30-44 also mostly voted Democrat, but about 52% of Wisconsinites aged 45-64 voted Republican. People 65 and older were more likely to vote Democrat this election. “Elections remind us how divided we can be, but also how much we all have at stake. So for me, it's bigger than which party wins. It's more about what happens afterward. Are we addressing the issues that everyday people face? Are we creating opportunities for young people and families? I feel like those are the kind of things every politician promises, but how can you make me feel it?” Nzegwu said, adding that he was enthusiastic to witness the election of the state’s first Black governor. “Wisconsin’s election is particularly significant because we’re witnessing history. Regardless of the political affiliation, that’s a milestone to be recognized. … I think the representation is just the beginning,” Nzegwu said. “What matters now is how the leadership translates into meaningful progress for Wisconsin. I honestly believe that Crowley has displayed that through his entire campaign, and I’m excited to see how we move forward and bridge the political differences.” The Cap Times welcomes tips from readers to help us inform our community. Email tips@captimes.com or visit captimes.com/tips for more options. Dane County Executive Melissa Agard said in a statement the results of the Nov. 3 election represent “important milestones for our state and reflect the diversity and strength of the people of Wisconsin.” Agard congratulated Senate Democratic Leader Dianne Hesselbein and Assembly Democratic Leader Greta Neubauer for leading the charge to secure Democratic majorities in both chambers of the Wisconsin Legislature. “Last night, Wisconsin made history, and I couldn’t be more excited about what comes next,” Agard wrote. “Congratulations to Governor-elect David Crowley on his historic victory, (reelected) Attorney General Josh Kaul, (Lt. Gov.-elect) Sarah Godlewski, (Secretary of State-elect) Jocasta Zamarripa, and (State Treasurer-elect) Yee Leng Xiong.” Zamarripa became the first Latina and first openly bi member of both the state Legislature and the Milwaukee City Council. Xiong is the first Hmong American to serve in a statewide office. “Beyond the historic nature of these victories, the people of Wisconsin sent a clear message. Folks want a government that works for everyday people, not just the wealthiest among us. They want their elected leaders focused on the issues that matter most in their daily lives, from affordable housing and quality education to accessible healthcare and economic opportunity,” Agard added. Dana Pellebon, executive director of the RCC Sexual Violence Resource Center in Madison, said the path forward will require collaboration and more voter education on how agencies and government entities work, especially surrounding state-funded survivor services, and behavioral and mental health programs at the local level. “We are really looking at things like the Attorney General's Office race, because the Attorney General's Office also determines the direction of how (sexual assault) survivors are treated in spaces and how much coordination is happening between advocates, law enforcement and courts,” she said. “For folks like us who are doing groundwork with our most vulnerable populations, these elections matter in ways that are not evident when you are reading the newspapers,” Pellebon said. “It’s important to have people in the Legislature who understand why certain policies are needed outside of politics and personal beliefs, but who are more focused on what is best for the people in Wisconsin to keep us moving forward, because we're not moving forward.” Signs signify to voters the polling place at Trinity Lutheran Church in Madison. Other political leaders reflected on local needs regarding housing access, funding for services and programs, and public safety ahead of next year’s Spring Election when Madison voters will choose the next mayor and half of the City Council. Elected officials in Madison and Dane County said they hope newly elected state officials will prioritize funding for public education, housing and healthcare, and other local government services. Madison City Council member Regina Vidaver’s seat is up for reelection in April. She declined to comment on whether she’s running for a new term but said she’s thrilled at Tuesday’s election outcome and is hopeful for more support for growing municipalities. “With Democratic control of the state, we can finally fund our schools appropriately, taking the burden off the backs of property owners,” Vidaver said. She said she hopes Democrats will fully fund city services provided to state government, such as police and fire protection and infrastructure, “taking pressure off the budgets of Madison and other municipalities with a major state building presence,” Vidaver said. “I’m also hopeful the state’s shared revenue calculations will better reflect the population of the state, and give Madison back more of what we put in to the state’s coffers.” The Cap Times reached out to candidates running for Madison mayor next year and asked for their thoughts on how the Nov. 3 election will affect Madison’s local government. Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway announced she won’t seek reelection next year, and the candidate pool is deep. It includes former Madison City Council members Syed Abbas and Brian Benford, former Dane County Board member April Kigeya, One City Schools founder and CEO Kaleem Caire, hospitality and food service director Larry Williams, Monkey Bar Gym founder Jonny Hinds, and former Golden Gloves boxer and east side bartender Marcus Johnson. Johnson said the recent state election proved the power of Wisconsin’s voters amid the “failed leadership” in the White House under Donald Trump. “Now more than ever, people are paying attention to politicians, and the Trump regime really paid for all of its negative rhetoric being parroted by politicians, whose bottom line is the almighty dollar,” Johnson said. Abbas said partisan state politics have delayed progress on transit and public health, and he expressed hope for more collaborative, progressive state leadership under the Democratic trifecta. “We need to reinvest in a community big time and give communities more local control, so we can create our own rent control programs. We can work with our community, our businesses. Sometimes, the city of Madison is very restrictive about what they can and cannot do under the state statute. So there's a lot at stake here for Madison and Dane County both,” Abbas said. Kigeya said the election results are worth celebrating, but people are still struggling with housing, the cost of living, access to mental health services, and “simply feeling like they have a seat at the table.” “Last night was one of those nights that reminded me why I got involved in public service in the first place. I sat with my children watching history unfold, and I was genuinely emotional. Not just because of who won, but because of what those victories represent,” she said. “We’re living in a time when so many people feel unheard, overlooked, and quite frankly, exhausted by politics. I think last night reminded people that their voices still have power.” Caire said he finally saw the vision the national Democratic Party had held for years and that Wisconsin is part of the movement. Looking ahead to the mayoral race, he said the question on the ballot will be “what kind of community is Madison going to be?” “Traditional Madison – Old Madison – has to get over his fear of change,” Caire said. “New Madison has to recognize that when you come here, there are people who are here, who have aspirations, who have needs, who have goals. … If we're going to be a part of that big future, that future that embraces diversity and embraces inclusion, vote for them.”
